do-ebay-returns-wipe-the-profit.html.text:
← eBay fee calculator

A 10% return rate can erase a thin eBay listing

Resellers search for “eBay return rate profit” because the number on a completed sale is not the number that hits the bank account. eBay’s Money Back Guarantee and buyer-friendly returns mean a slice of orders come back. The item is often still sellable. The outbound label is not.

On a typical example — a $40 item, $6 shipping charged, 13.6% final value fee, $0.40 fixed fee, $12 cost of goods, a $5 outbound label, and $1 of packaging — the completed sale leaves about $21.34. If that order is returned, the buyer is refunded, fees are often refunded, and the item comes back. You still paid the $5 label and $1 packaging, plus whatever return postage you cover. At a $5 return label that is $11 gone. Mix nine completed sales with one return and the expected profit is no longer $21.34.

Promoted-listings fees are frequently not refunded. If that applies to you, lower the “fees refunded on return” field instead of pretending every fee comes back. The calculator does not decide eBay’s current refund policy.

Open the eBay fee calculator, enter the rates from your statements and the return rate you actually see, and read three figures: expected profit after returns, cash one return still eats, and the return rate that takes expected profit to zero. Then use the repricing table to see whether a higher list price still helps after that rate. A single opened case is a different question — whether a partial refund still beats taking that return.

This is arithmetic, not advice. It does not forecast your category return rate or claim a listing is safe to keep.

Common questions

Do eBay returns wipe seller profit?

They can. A completed sale keeps the profit after fees and cost of goods. A return typically refunds the buyer and often refunds final value fees, but the outbound label, packaging, and return postage usually stay with the seller. Expected profit is the completed-sale profit mixed with that return loss at the return rate you enter.

What return rate still leaves a profit on eBay?

The break-even return rate is the highest rate at which expected profit is still zero. It depends on the completed-sale profit and how much cash one return still eats. Enter your fees, shipping, and expected return rate in the free calculator; it is arithmetic, not a forecast of your category.

Enter the sale price, the fee rates your own account is charged, what you paid for the item, and what shipping costs you. The rates come from the boxes you fill in rather than a stored fee table, so the arithmetic stays right when eBay changes a category rate, or when your store tier changes what you pay.

Why does a sale that looked profitable still leave me short?

Because most of what erodes an eBay sale lands after checkout, not in the list price: the outbound label, return postage on the ones that come back, promoted-listing bills that are charged whether or not the click was the reason it sold, and the time spent packing. Does offering free shipping cost me money?

Should I offer an eBay coupon?

← eBay fee & profit calculator

This calculator vs. a spreadsheet

A seller who tracks eBay profit more than a few times usually ends up with a spreadsheet: a price cell, a cost cell, and one fee-percentage cell subtracted from the total. That formula is right for the simple case and silently wrong the moment a sale is more than the simple case — which, on eBay, is often. This page names no specific product; it compares against the generic method of tracking fees and profit in a spreadsheet or by hand.

A spreadsheet can multiply an order total by one fee rate and subtract cost of goods in a single formula, and many sellers already have one. What it does not do on its own is stack Promoted Listings and international fees on top of the final value fee when a sale carries either, or price what a typed return rate costs once the outbound label, packaging, and any unrefunded fees are counted — so a "13.6% fee" cell quietly understates the real fee bill on any promoted or international sale, and a completed-sale profit column quietly overstates what a batch of orders actually nets once some come back.

This calculator takes the final value rate, the Promoted Listings rate, and the international fee rate as separate inputs and stacks them the way eBay actually charges them, on the full order total including shipping charged. It also takes an expected return rate, return shipping cost, and the share of fees eBay refunds on a return, and reports both completed-sale profit and return-adjusted expected profit side by side — plus the exact price that hits a target margin, a target profit dollar amount, or a target ROI, solved backward rather than guessed and rechecked by hand.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What does this order net at one flat fee rate, no returns?Either one — that is the simple case both get right.
What does it net once Promoted Listings and an international rate stack on top?This calculator — on the $40 item / $6 shipping default, adding an 8% Promoted rate and a 1.65% international rate lowers completed profit from $21.34 to $16.91, a $4.44 gap a single fee-rate cell does not show.
What does a typed return rate actually cost?This calculator's return-adjusted expected profit — at 10% returns on the base case, profit drops from $21.34 completed to $18.11 expected, because a return still eats the outbound label, packaging, and any unrefunded fees.
What price hits a target margin, profit dollar, or ROI?This calculator solves backward for it automatically; a spreadsheet needs its own goal-seek or a manually rebuilt formula.
Is a batch of several units still solved correctly?This calculator spreads the one per-order fixed fee across the batch while keeping per-unit costs multiplied — a copied-down spreadsheet row often double-counts or drops the per-order fee.
I already have a working profit sheet and don't want to change tools.Keep it — this calculator is a free second check, not a replacement for a system you maintain.

What this page is not

This calculator is not a bookkeeping system and does not track listings or orders over time; a spreadsheet or a seller platform still does that job better. What it replaces is the one-off arithmetic of stacking eBay's fee types correctly and pricing a return rate on a single order — the part of a profit sheet most likely to be approximated as "revenue times one fee percentage" because modeling Promoted Listings, international fees, and returns correctly, every time terms change, is tedious enough that most sheets skip it.

Common questions

Can a spreadsheet work out eBay profit?

Yes, for the simple case: revenue times one fee percentage, minus cost of goods and shipping. Most sellers already have a cell like that. It stops being right the moment Promoted Listings or an international sale add their own percentage on top of the final value fee, or a return comes back and eats the outbound label and packaging while only partially refunding fees — none of which fits a single fee-rate cell without rebuilding the formula.

Where does a hand-built eBay profit sheet usually go wrong?

Two places, on the calculator's own defaults. First, treating 13.6% as the whole fee: adding an 8% Promoted Listings rate and a 1.65% international rate on the same $40 item plus $6 shipping order lowers completed-sale profit from $21.34 to $16.91 — a $4.44 gap one flat-rate cell never shows. Second, never pricing returns: a 10% expected return rate on the base case lowers profit from $21.34 completed to $18.11 expected, because a return still eats the outbound shipping, packaging, and any unrefunded portion of the fees already paid, and a spreadsheet that only tracks completed sales has no row for that.

What does a spreadsheet not check for you?

Whether Promoted Listings and international fees are stacking on top of the final value fee rather than replacing it; what a typed return rate actually costs once the outbound label, packaging, and unrefunded fees are counted; the exact price that hits a target margin or profit dollar amount, solved backward rather than guessed and rechecked; and return on the cash actually invested, which is smaller than the invoice total because fees are deducted from proceeds rather than paid up front.

Does either one know what eBay will actually charge?

No. Both this calculator and a spreadsheet apply the fee rates you type in. Neither reproduces eBay's live, category-specific rate card — verify current rates against eBay's own Fee Calculator in Seller Center or a recent invoice before relying on either.

Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator this page links to runs entirely in your browser; nothing you type is uploaded.
